\chapter{Mine and Yours}
\label{ch:it-possessivi}
\hlchaptermodality{34}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say whose something is, keep the article Italian keeps and drop it where Italian drops it, address somebody as signore or signora, and put a pronoun after a preposition.}

The chapter's last lesson gives the stressed pronouns somewhere to stand. No preposition in this book had ever taken a pronoun after it, and per — Chapter 32's — is what makes per me sayable.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mio, tuo, suo]{mio, tuo, suo — my, your, his and hers}

\label{lesson:IT-C34-mio-tuo-suo}



\begin{quote}
A new chapter, opening the second column this book has left completely empty.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{qui / lì} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{questo} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{non} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{rosso, blu} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the three, and their endings}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{mio} — my · \textbf{tuo} — your \emph{(to one person, informally)} · \textbf{suo} — his, her, its
\end{quote}

They are describing words, and they take the four endings every describing word takes, agreeing with \textbf{the thing owned} and never with the owner:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{my} — mio · mia · miei · mie
  \item \textbf{your} — tuo · tua · tuoi · tue
  \item \textbf{his / her} — suo · sua · suoi · sue
\end{itemize}

\emph{(The masculine plurals \textbf{miei}, \textbf{tuoi}, \textbf{suoi} are the one irregular corner.)}

Read the middle sentence of that paragraph again, because it is the thing English speakers get wrong for years. \textbf{Suo} does not tell you whether the owner is a man or a woman. It tells you about the thing owned:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{la sua amica} — his friend, or her friend. The \textbf{-a} is \emph{amica}'s.
\end{quote}

English chooses \emph{his} or \emph{her} by the owner. Italian chooses \emph{suo} or \emph{sua} by the possession. If you must say whose, Italian adds \emph{di lui} or \emph{di lei} afterwards.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Mio, tuo, suo} are Latin \textbf{meus, tuus, suus}, barely changed.

Now a correction. The \textbf{mi chiamo} lesson gave you that phrase, and its \emph{mi} is \textbf{not} a possessive. \emph{Mi chiamo} is not \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{}; it is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I call myself}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{mi} is the reflexive \emph{myself}, and \emph{chiamo} is \emph{I call}. It looks like \emph{mio} and is a different word doing a different job.

Which is why, until this line, you could give your name and could not say \textbf{my name}. That is the next lesson but one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mio, mia, miei, mie}
  \item \emph{tuo, tua}
  \item \emph{suo, sua}
  \item \emph{la sua amica}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \emph{suo} agree with the owner or the thing owned? (\textbf{The thing owned} — \emph{la sua amica} is his friend or her friend.) What is the \emph{mi} of \emph{mi chiamo}? (\textbf{Not a possessive} — the reflexive \emph{myself}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nostro, vostro]{nostro, vostro — ours and yours}

\label{lesson:IT-C34-nostro-vostro}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, and a long throw to the age question.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mio, tuo, suo} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{quello} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{non capisco} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{avere} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the plural owners}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{nostro} — our · \textbf{vostro} — your \emph{(to more than one person)}
\end{quote}

Same four endings, same rule — they agree with the thing owned:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{our} — nostro · nostra · nostri · nostre
  \item \textbf{your (to several)} — vostro · vostra · vostri · vostre
\end{itemize}

No irregular corner here: they behave exactly like \emph{buono} and \emph{primo}.

The set is now complete except for \textbf{loro}, \textquotedblleft{}their\textquotedblright{}, which never changes at all — \emph{il loro amico}, \emph{la loro amica}, \emph{i loro amici}. One shape for everything.

You already hold \emph{loro} as a subject pronoun. The \textbf{essere} table printed \emph{noi siamo · voi siete · loro sono} and then warned you that \emph{io sono} and \emph{loro sono} are identical, telling you to keep \emph{loro} where the context would not settle it. That is the same word: Italian's \textquotedblleft{}they\textquotedblright{} and its \textquotedblleft{}their\textquotedblright{} are one shape.

\begin{cousinweb}
Turn back to the very first lesson. \textbf{Ciao} was traced there to the Venetian greeting \textbf{s-ciào vostro} — \textquotedblleft{}{[}I am{]} \textbf{your} slave\textquotedblright{}, a servant's formula that wore down into the friendliest word in the language.

That \textbf{vostro} was glossed, in the very first lesson you read, as \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{your}\textquotedblright{}. It was never named as a word you could pick up and use, because at that point you could not use anything. You can now, and you have had it all along: the word for \emph{your} has been sitting inside \emph{ciao} for a hundred and thirty lessons.

\emph{Nostro} and \emph{vostro} are Latin \textbf{noster} and \textbf{vester}, and English took the first of them, through French, in \textbf{paternoster} — \emph{pater noster}, \textquotedblleft{}our father.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nostro, nostra, nostri, nostre}
  \item \emph{vostro, vostra}
  \item \emph{il loro amico}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}our\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}your (to several people).\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Nostro}} — \emph{\textbf{vostro}}.) Which word of this book has carried \emph{vostro} from its first page? (\emph{\textbf{Ciao}}, from \emph{s-ciào vostro}.) Which possessive never changes? (\emph{\textbf{Loro}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[il mio nome]{il mio nome — the article the possessive keeps}

\label{lesson:IT-C34-il-mio-nome}



\begin{quote}
The chapter's middle lesson, and it introduces no new word.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nostro, vostro} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{questo caffè} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{né … né} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ho venti anni} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the article stays}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{il mio nome} — my name · \textbf{la mia amica} — my friend · \textbf{il tuo caffè} — your coffee
\end{quote}

Here is the rule, and it is the one thing about Italian possessives that has to be learnt rather than guessed:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{The possessive does not replace the article. It sits between the article and the noun.}
\end{quote}

That is the opposite of the demonstrative rule you learnt one chapter ago. \emph{Questo} \textbf{evicts} the article — \emph{questo caffè}, never \emph{questo il caffè}. \emph{Mio} \textbf{keeps} it:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
demonstrative & \textbf{questo} caffè \emph{(no article)} \\
possessive & \textbf{il mio} caffè \emph{(article stays)} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English drops it and so does Spanish — \emph{my name}, \emph{mi nombre} — so both an English speaker and a Spanish speaker will leave it out for a while. Italian wants all three words.

\textbf{This lesson introduces no new word.} \emph{Il, la, lo} is the first chapter's; \emph{nome} is the people chapter's; \emph{mio} and \emph{tuo} are two lessons back. Until now you could say your name and could not say the words \textbf{my name}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: the exception, one family and no article}]
There is exactly one place the article goes, and Italians use it constantly:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{mio fratello} — my brother · \textbf{mia sorella} — my sister \textbf{mio padre} — my father · \textbf{mia madre} — my mother
\end{quote}

\textbf{A singular, unmodified family member takes no article.} \emph{Il fratello} and \emph{la sorella} are the family chapter's, and so are \emph{il padre} and \emph{la madre}. Put a possessive in front of one of them and the article drops out.

Three conditions, and all three must hold:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{singular} — the plural takes it back: \textbf{i miei fratelli}
  \item \textbf{unmodified} — add a describing word and it comes back: \textbf{il mio primo fratello}
  \item \textbf{not loro} — \emph{loro} always keeps it: \textbf{il loro fratello}
\end{enumerate}

So: \textbf{mio fratello}, but \textbf{i miei fratelli}, but \textbf{il loro fratello}. It is the one corner of the Italian possessive that has to be memorised, and every Italian child gets it right without being taught, because the family words are said far too often to get wrong.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{il mio nome}
  \item \emph{la mia amica}
  \item \emph{mio fratello}
  \item \emph{i miei fratelli}
  \item \emph{il loro fratello}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my name.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Il mio nome}} — with the article.) Say \textquotedblleft{}my brother.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Mio fratello}} — without it.) Name the three conditions for dropping the article. (\textbf{Singular, unmodified, and not} \emph{\textbf{loro}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[signore, signora]{signore, signora — sir and madam, and speaking to somebody by name}

\label{lesson:IT-C34-signore-signora}



\begin{quote}
Four in, and this one finishes what the formal address started.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{il mio nome} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Questo è Marco} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{anche / neanche} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ho parlato} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the two titles}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{signore} — sir, Mr · \textbf{signora} — madam, Mrs · \textbf{signorina} — miss
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Buongiorno, signora.} — Good morning, madam. \textbf{Come sta, signore?} — How are you, sir? \textbf{Arrivederci, signora.}
\end{quote}

This book taught you the formal \textbf{Lei} and the whole \emph{come sta} / \emph{come stai} contrast, and then gave you nothing to put after it. That is an odd shape: a course that teaches formality and not the words formality is normally carried in. Here they are.

\textbf{The one rule that catches people.} Before a surname, \emph{signore} loses its final \textbf{-e}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{il signor Rossi} — Mr Rossi \emph{(not il signore Rossi)} \textbf{la signora Rossi} — Mrs Rossi \emph{(signora keeps its -a)}
\end{quote}

That is the same shortening you met on the first page, where \textbf{buono} becomes \textbf{buon} in \emph{buongiorno}. Italian drops a final vowel before another word far more readily than English does.

\emph{Signorina} is going out of use for the reason \emph{Miss} is, and \textbf{signora} is the safe choice for any adult woman.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: speaking to somebody, by name or by title}]
Put the person you are speaking \textbf{to} at the front or the end of what you say, with a comma. Italian calls this the \emph{vocativo}, and it needs no other machinery:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Marco, buongiorno.} · \textbf{Buongiorno, Marco.} \textbf{Signora, come sta?} · \textbf{Come sta, signora?}
\end{quote}

Nothing in this book had ever done this. Every practice exchange in it opens with a bare greeting and never with a name, so a learner could greet a stranger and not a friend — which is backwards, since it is the friend whose name you know.

One thing Italian does \textbf{not} do here, and English speakers transfer it by mistake: \textbf{the article goes.} \emph{Il signor Rossi} is how you talk \textbf{about} him; \textbf{Signor Rossi}, with no \emph{il}, is how you talk \textbf{to} him.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{signore, signora}
  \item \emph{Buongiorno, signora.}
  \item \emph{il signor Rossi}
  \item \emph{Marco, buongiorno.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}good morning, madam.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Buongiorno, signora}}.) What happens to \emph{signore} before a surname? (\textbf{It drops its} \emph{\textbf{-e}} — \emph{il signor Rossi}.) Which word from the first page shortens the same way? (\emph{\textbf{Buono}} \textbf{$\to$} \emph{\textbf{buon}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[per me, a te]{per me — the pronouns that go after a preposition}

\label{lesson:IT-C34-per-me}



\begin{quote}
The chapter's last lesson, and its longest throw is to the remote past.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{signore, signora} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{qui / lì} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{c'è / ci sono} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{parlò} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a second set of pronouns}
\begin{quote}
after a preposition, Italian uses \textbf{me, te, lui, lei, noi, voi, loro}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{per me} — for me · \textbf{per te} — for you · \textbf{per lui} — for him \textbf{Un caffè per me.} \textbf{Questo è per te.} — This is for you.
\end{quote}

Look at what changed and what did not. \emph{Io} and \emph{tu} become \textbf{me} and \textbf{te}; everything else — \emph{lui, lei, noi, voi, loro} — is the same word the conjugation tables have been printing all along. Only the first two persons have a second shape.

These are called the \textbf{stressed} pronouns, and stress is the honest name for them: they are the ones you can shout, the ones a preposition can lean on, and the ones that stand alone in an answer:

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{Chi prende il caffè?} — \textbf{Io.} \emph{(subject: the subject form)} — \textbf{Per chi è?} — \textbf{Per me.} \emph{(after a preposition: the stressed form)}
\end{quote}

The one to watch is \textbf{a}, the preposition this book has used all along in \emph{a Roma} and \emph{a domani}. Put a person after it and you get \textbf{a me}, \textbf{a te}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens: a me piace, and where the weight falls}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{A me piace il caffè.} — I like coffee.
\end{quote}

Compare the \textbf{mi piace} you already have. The meaning is the same; the \emph{a me} version puts the weight on \textbf{me}, and it is what an Italian reaches for when contradicting somebody:

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{Non mi piace il caffè.} — \textbf{A me piace.} — Well, \emph{I} like it.
\end{quote}

The \emph{mi} of \emph{mi piace} is the unstressed shape and cannot be emphasised at all — you cannot say it louder and mean anything by it. \emph{A me} is how Italian shouts a pronoun: not by raising the voice, but by swapping in the other set.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{per me, per te, per lui}
  \item \emph{Questo è per te.}
  \item \emph{A me piace il caffè.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the first two stressed pronouns? (\emph{\textbf{Me}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{te}}.) Which of the others change? (\textbf{None} — \emph{lui, lei, noi, voi, loro} stay.) Say \textquotedblleft{}this is for you.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Questo è per te}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
